status_summary: The Justice Department is examining its FARA regulations, but not in a China-focused way and with mixed direction. The Attorney General's charging memorandum of 2025-02-05 limited criminal FARA and 18 U.S.C. 951 charges to conduct similar to traditional espionage by foreign government actors, disbanded the Foreign Influence Task Force and directed the Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, including its FARA Unit, toward civil enforcement, regulatory initiatives and public guidance. National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (signed 2025-09-25) directed Joint Terrorism Task Forces to investigate nongovernmental organizations and others with foreign ties suspected of FARA violations connected to domestic political violence; it does not mention China. DOJ's proposed FARA rule of 2025-01-02, which would both narrow and broaden different exemptions and expand labeling, was not among the rulemakings DOJ withdrew on 2025-09-11, and the 2026 Unified Agenda (published 2026-08-14) lists a National Security Division final FARA rule under consideration; law-firm alerts of 2026-08-14 and 2026-09-28 report that it would adopt many but not all of the proposals and broaden exemptions commonly relied on by companies and law firms, with no target date, and no final rule has been issued. DOJ's June 2026 notices revising the FARA registration forms state that they are not part of that rulemaking. Senators reintroduced two Lobbying Disclosure Act bills on 2025-03-06 addressing the LDA exemption from FARA registration. DOJ continued Section 951 prosecutions involving agents of the PRC government in 2025 and 2026, which is enforcement rather than a review of FARA authorities. No China-specific or economic-espionage FARA examination or rule was found.

timeline.event: DOJ published a proposed rule amending FARA regulations (comment deadline 2025-03-03), with mixed changes to the commercial and legal representation exemptions and expanded labeling for digital media; published before the tracking period.

The Attorney General's memorandum on charging policy limited criminal FARA and Section 951 charges to conduct similar to traditional espionage by foreign government actors, disbanded the Foreign Influence Task Force and directed the Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, including its FARA Unit, to focus on civil enforcement, regulatory initiatives and public guidance.

Senators reintroduced the Lobbying Disclosure Improvement Act and the Disclosing Foreign Influence in Lobbying Act, which address the Lobbying Disclosure Act exemption from FARA registration and foreign-government direction of lobbying.
DOJ withdrew several dozen proposed rulemakings as part of a deregulatory initiative; the FARA proposed rule (RIN 1124-AA00) was not among them.

National Security Presidential Memorandum 7, Countering Domestic Terrorism and Organized Political Violence (published 2025-09-30), directed Joint Terrorism Task Forces to investigate nongovernmental organizations and others with ties to foreign governments or influence networks suspected of FARA violations or money laundering connected to domestic political violence; it does not mention China or economic espionage.

DOJ's FARA Unit published notices seeking OMB approval of revised FARA registration forms (NSD-1 through NSD-6); the notices state that they do not concern the pending FARA proposed rule and do not describe the changes.

A law-firm alert reported that the August 2026 Unified Agenda entry says DOJ's National Security Division is considering a final FARA rule adopting many, but not all, of the January 2025 proposals, expected to broaden exemptions relied on by corporations and law firms; no target date was given.

A law-firm alert reported that no final FARA rule had been issued, described DOJ Section 951 cases involving agents of the PRC government (including a guilty plea on 2026-05-29), and noted a DOJ press release of 2026-09-16 reminding the public of civil and criminal liability under FARA and Section 951.

title: Examine Foreign Agents Registration Act loopholes to counter Chinese economic espionage
uncertainties: Stage is proposed: the Mandate asks only that FARA authorities and loopholes be examined and addressed with the Attorney General to counter China's economic espionage. DOJ's retained rulemaking and the 2026 Unified Agenda entry are an announced examination of FARA rules, but their direction is mixed (the proposal narrows the commercial exemption while broadening the legal exemption and labeling scope, and the reported final rule is expected to broaden some exemptions) and not China-specific, so the match is parallel; the 2025 Lobbying Disclosure Act bills are introduced proposals. Rule applied: diverged needs an operative action running opposite to the text. The charging memorandum narrows criminal FARA use generally but keeps it for espionage-like conduct by foreign government actors, NSPM-7 widens FARA investigations in a different, domestic context, DOJ continued Section 951 cases involving the PRC, and the broader exemptions exist only in a planned final rule; none is an operative step opposite to the text, and none addresses FARA loopholes, so in_progress does not apply either. Judgment: if a final rule broadens exemptions with no China-related tightening, diverged should be reconsidered. The memorandum was read on justice.gov in this review, replacing the earlier law-firm-hosted copy. The Unified Agenda entry itself was not read; it is known from a Federal Register search excerpt and law-firm alerts. Section 6712 of Public Law 119-60 (policy toward certain agents of foreign governments) was read by title only, because the committee copy's text ends within Sec. 6703. The Senate intelligence committee's FY2027 bill (S. 4615, reported 2026-05-20) lists sections on the definition of foreign instrumentality for the economic espionage statute and on trade secret protection, which are not FARA and were read by title only. No overlap with chapter 17 records was found.
